newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM takes swipe at foreign investor critics.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM takes swipe at foreign investor critics.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus admitted on Tuesday his government had been slow in pushing for stricter capital markets regulation but took a swipe at foreigners complaining about losses on the Prague bourse.

Speaking at an economic conference, Klaus said the cabinet would stick to its April plan to clean up the markets and bring them closer to western standards but said he was still hesitant about excessive regulation.

He added that many foreign investors, critical of Czech capital markets, had bought into Czech investment funds at large discounts, lost money and "now are crying for help" because they had failed to accurately assess the risks.
"There is no doubt that capital markets are different from ordinary markets and that they need more government intervention or regulation than ordinary markets," Klaus said.

But he added: "I am not very optimistic about regulation in general and about regulation of capital markets in particular." While the stock market has come in for most criticism, there have also been complaints about fixed income markets.
Klaus said that there seemed to be insufficient demand for shares to prompt disclosure by companies, but noted that delayed legislation may have contributed.

Belatedly responding to widespread investor and media criticism, the cabinet in April agreed to set up an independent markets oversight body to strengthen market regulation, and it pledged to separate investment units of banks from their commercial arms.
Analysts and investors, who have been turning away from the Czech market in droves, welcomed the moves but said they would wait to see what Klaus's administration actually achieves.
Since hitting a year high of 629 on February 26, the PX50 index on the Prague bourse has since fallen by almost 20 percent.
Klaus said investors from abroad should have better analysed the risks involved in Czech investment funds which at one point were trading at 70-80 percent discounts to net asset values.

"To a discriminating investor this would clearly indicate a specific risk which the market placed on such an investment. Regardless of this warning, they bought into these funds and now are crying for help. We were inexperienced and innocent, they should not have been."
Klaus's partners at the panel discussion, including World Bank vice-President Joseph Stiglitz, responded saying that such a risk in assets management was a historical and worldwide rarity.
"The discounts mean that people entrusted with assets are able to take 80 percent of it away - a system which is not able to prevent that really raises questions," Stiglitz said.

"(Such a discount) implies a risk that is higher than in any country in the world. That is not a good situation and it is a sign that something is wrong," added Stephen Ross, Professor of Finance at Yale University and Director of Ross and Roll Asset Management.
